analysis.one_liner: Seals photos of detainee treatment by U.S. forces after 9/11 from public records requests.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a House vote, but nearly identical language was attached to a war funding bill and signed into law in June 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Secretary of Defense certify that releasing photos of how U.S. forces treated detainees after 9/11 would endanger Americans or troops. Once certified, those photos could never be pried loose through the Freedom of Information Act, the main legal tool citizens use to see government records. Certifications would expire after three years but could be renewed indefinitely. The government could still release the photos voluntarily if it chose to.
analysis.who_benefits: The Defense Department and other agencies holding the photographs, and the officials whose conduct the images document, gain a legal shield against forced public release. The bill's stated purpose is protecting U.S. citizens and deployed personnel from endangerment.
analysis.who_benefits_short: The Pentagon and officials it shields

how_it_helps.text: Exempts any photograph of detainee treatment taken between September 11, 2001 and January 22, 2009 from disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act once the Secretary of Defense certifies that release would endanger U.S. citizens, troops, or deployed government employees.
Allows the Secretary of Defense to renew a certification any number of times, so the three-year expiration can be extended repeatedly, while requiring only notice to Congress — not approval.
Leaves the government free to release any covered photo voluntarily, so the secrecy applies only against citizens suing for access, not against the government's own choices.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary citizens, journalists, and victims seeking to know what was done in their name. Freedom of Information Act requests are how the public holds the government to account; this bill closes that route for a defined set of records regardless of the merits of any individual request.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public's right to government records

drawbacks.text: The exemption is blanket and retroactive: it covers photographs already in existence, including any depicting abuse, and removes the case-by-case balancing that FOIA normally applies before withholding a record.
The three-year expiration offers little protection because the Secretary of Defense can renew a certification any number of times, indefinitely keeping the same photographs sealed.

The public loses the ability to independently verify how detainees were treated and whether misconduct was addressed, since the institution being scrutinized is the one deciding whether release would be 'endangering.'

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Protecting troops and citizens from real endangerment is a legitimate concern, and FOIA already lets agencies withhold records on those grounds after adversarial review. This bill replaces that check with a self-issued, indefinitely renewable exemption written by the institution whose conduct is at issue. The transparency and accountability cost outweighs the security benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two committees and never received a vote, but Congress attached nearly identical language to a war funding bill that the President signed in June 2009, so the substance became law without the House ever voting on it as a standalone bill.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on June 15, 2009 and referred to the Oversight and Government Reform and Armed Services Committees; the public record shows no markup, no vote, and no further action in either committee before the Congress ended.

The bill would have allowed the Secretary of Defense to exempt photos of detainee treatment from FOIA by certifying that disclosure would endanger Americans or troops, with renewable three-year certifications.
All 75 cosponsors were House Republicans, joining the Republican sponsor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Defense Department and the agencies holding the photographs came out ahead: they received the secrecy this bill promised through an amendment to the must-pass war funding bill, while the public lost the FOIA route to the images without ever seeing a standalone vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Pentagon and its record-holding agencies

for.name: K. Michael Conaway
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt detainee treatment photographs from FOIA disclosure.

for.name: 75 of 178 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the full cosponsor list was Republican.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Signed a war funding bill containing nearly identical detainee-photo secrecy language into law in June 2009, achieving the substance of the bill without a standalone vote.

against.name: Ike Skelton
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration after its referral; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: Edolphus Towns
against.role: Chair, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration after its referral; the record shows no committee action.

against.name: American Civil Liberties Union
against.what_they_did: Its Freedom of Information Act lawsuit seeking release of the detainee photographs was the litigation this bill was written to override; the organization opposed suppressing the images.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a House Republican (75 of 178), with no Democrats signing on; however, the Democratic-led Senate attached nearly identical language to a war funding bill and the Democratic president signed it, so the bill's substance was not strictly a Republican project.

industries.note: The bill exempts photographs of detainee treatment from FOIA, shielding the very institutions whose conduct the images document from public scrutiny. The certification decision rests with the Secretary of Defense — the party being scrutinized — and can be renewed indefinitely.
FOIA requesters, including news organizations and civil-liberties litigants, lose the legal avenue to obtain the photographs. Their loss of access is the public's loss of accountability.
